note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: Spark streaming in milliseconds: Real-Time Mode is GA for Declarative Pipelines
items.summary: On 29 October Databricks made Real-Time Mode generally available on Spark Declarative Pipelines. Instead of running a micro-batch every few seconds, all stages run at once and rows move on as soon as they are produced. Databricks reports millisecond latencies. You turn it on with a continuous pipeline, the realTimeMode setting and an update flow with the RealTime trigger.
items.why: The classic interview answer, 'Spark for seconds, Flink for milliseconds', is now incomplete. A senior answer names the trade-off: Real-Time Mode keeps one engine and one skill set for batch and stream, while Flink still has the most mature event-time and large-state handling.
items.try: In module 5's streaming lab, write down the latency budget for each sink (dashboard, fraud check, lake table) and mark which ones need sub-second results. That decides whether Real-Time Mode is worth its always-on cost.

items.title: Serverless cost control moves to permissions on compute objects
items.summary: On 29 October Databricks made Serverless Compute Access Controls generally available. Each workspace gets default serverless compute objects for interactive work and for jobs and pipelines, with Can Use and Can Manage permissions like SQL warehouses. Size limits (S to XL) are in beta, and system.billing.usage gains a serverless_compute_id column for attribution.
items.why: Cluster policies controlled cost by limiting machines. With serverless there are no machines to limit, so cost governance becomes 'who may use which compute, up to what size', plus attribution. Expect this in platform and FinOps design questions.
items.try: Using the cost questions in module 7, sketch two compute objects (ad hoc analysts, production jobs) with their groups, size caps and a budget alert, and write the query that reports spend per object from the billing table.

items.title: Snowflake adds Time Travel and version tags for Iceberg tables
items.summary: Since 28 October (Preview), Snowflake can query a historical snapshot of an Apache Iceberg table by timestamp, snapshot ID, reference or version tag. A version tag such as audit_2026_q1 keeps a snapshot queryable for a set period, whatever the table's retention. GET_TABLE_VERSIONS and GET_TABLE_VERSION_REFS list snapshots and tags.
items.why: Reproducing a past report ('show me exactly what we published at quarter end') is a common senior interview question. Named, retained snapshots on an open table format answer it without copying data.
items.try: In module 2's storage lab, tag the snapshot after a load, run an update, then query both the tag and the current table and compare the row counts.

items.title: Secondary indexes are generally available in Snowflake
items.summary: Since 26 October, standard Snowflake tables can have secondary indexes on columns or expressions. They map values to the micro-partitions that hold them, speeding up selective point lookups and range queries, and can answer covered queries directly. Upkeep is automatic and billed as search optimization. Iceberg tables are not supported.
items.why: The usual line is that warehouses rely on pruning instead of indexes. That is still mostly true, but you now have one more lever for lookup-heavy workloads such as customer-service queries, with a write and maintenance cost you have to justify.
items.try: Revisit module D1's section on indexes and write one paragraph comparing clustering keys, search optimization and a secondary index for 'find all orders for one customer ID'.

items.title: Agentic document parsing in a single SQL call
items.summary: On 28 October Snowflake added an AGENTIC mode to AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT (Public Preview). It classifies the visuals in a document (charts, diagrams, tables), chooses how to process each one, and returns one response with the text, the layout, summaries of the visuals and the extracted structured data.
items.why: Getting unstructured documents into tables (invoices, reports, manuals) is becoming a normal data-engineering task. The design questions are cost per page, how to evaluate extraction quality, and where to keep the raw document for reprocessing.
items.try: In module A5's RAG pipeline, list the checks you would run on parsed output before it is embedded: a sample of tables compared by hand, numbers matched against the source text, and a cost-per-page budget.
